title: Each vs. Every
explain: Both are used with singular verbs, but they differ in focus. Each focuses on individuals one by one, while Every treats all as a collective group.

usage.desc: Individual focus — can be a pronoun or adjective (used for 2 or more).
Group/collective focus — adjective only (used for 3 or more).

examples: ✓ Each student is ready.
✓ Every boy is present.
✗ Every of the students is here.

title: Both + Not → Neither…Nor
explain: When negating both subjects, never use Both…not. Always replace it with Neither…nor for correct and natural English.

usage.desc: Both Ram and Shyam are not going.
Neither Ram nor Shyam is going.

examples: ✓ Neither Ram nor Shyam is going.
✓ Neither the dog nor the cat is here.
✗ Both of them are not present.

title: Who / Whom / Which / That
explain: These relative pronouns replace nouns in sentences. Choosing the right one depends on whether the noun is a person, a thing, or how it functions in the clause.

usage.desc: Subject — for people and pets.
Object — for people only.
For things and wild animals.
Universal — people, animals, things. Use after: all, any, only, same, none, superlatives.

examples: ✓ The boy who came is my friend.
✓ Whom did you call? (Him = Whom)
✓ This is the same pen that I lost.
✓ The cat which ran away is mine.

title: Much vs. Many
explain: Much is used with uncountable nouns (things you can't count individually). Many is used with countable nouns (things with a clear plural form).

usage.desc: Uncountable nouns — water, sugar, time, money.
Countable nouns — pens, books, boys, students.

examples: ✓ How much water do you need?
✓ How many pens do you have?
✗ How many sugar is left?
trick: If you can count it → Many | If you can't → Much

title: Little / A Little / The Little
explain: All three are used with uncountable nouns, but they carry different meanings based on the context — negative, positive, or specific.

usage.desc: Almost none — negative idea (not enough).
Some — positive idea (a small but sufficient amount).
All of the small amount that exists — specific.

examples: ✓ Little milk was left, so I couldn't make tea.
✓ A little milk is still left — enough for one cup.
✓ The little milk that was left was spoiled.

title: Few / A Few / The Few
explain: All three are used with countable nouns. Just like Little/A Little/The Little, they indicate negative, positive, or specific quantity.

usage.desc: Almost none — negative idea.
Some — positive idea.
All of the limited group — specific.

examples: ✓ Few books were interesting in the library. (negative — hardly any)
✓ A few books caught my attention. (positive — some)
✓ The few books I had were enough to prepare.
trick: Few = Negative | A few = Positive | The few = Specific group

title: Some vs. Any
explain: Some is used in affirmative sentences, offers, and requests. Any is used in negative sentences and questions.

usage.desc: Positive statements, offers, polite requests.
Negative sentences and questions.

examples: ✓ I need some help. (positive)
✓ Can you give me some advice? (polite request)
✓ Do you have any sugar? (question)
✓ I don't have any time.

title: Since vs. For
explain: Since refers to a specific point in time (when something started). For refers to a duration — how long something has continued.

usage.desc: A specific starting point — since 5 PM, since 2019, since childhood.
A duration of time — for 2 hours, for 3 years, for a long time.

examples: ✓ I have been studying since 5 PM.
✓ I have been studying for 2 hours.
✗ I have been studying since 2 hours.

title: Who vs. Whom
explain: Who acts as the subject (doing the action). Whom acts as the object (receiving the action). Replace with He/Him to test.

usage.desc: Subject — replaces 'He/She' in the sentence.
Object — replaces 'Him/Her' in the sentence.

examples: ✓ Who called you? (He called → Who)
✓ Whom did you call? (You called him → Whom)
✗ Whom is calling me? (He is calling = Who)
trick: Replace with He → Who | Replace with Him → Whom

title: Fewer vs. Less
explain: Fewer is used with countable nouns (things you can count). Less is used with uncountable nouns (things measured in bulk).

usage.desc: Countable nouns — mistakes, students, chairs.
Uncountable nouns — sugar, water, time, effort.

examples: ✓ She made fewer mistakes in this test.
✓ I add less sugar to my tea now.
✗ She made less mistakes. (mistakes are countable)

title: Between vs. Among
explain: Between is used when referring to exactly two distinct items or people. Among is used when referring to three or more people or a group.

usage.desc: Exactly 2 items or people.
3 or more — a group or crowd.

examples: ✓ He divided the money between his two sons.
✓ There is a secret among the five friends.
✗ He sat between the three chairs.

title: Bring vs. Take
explain: The direction of movement matters. Bring means to carry something toward the speaker. Take means to carry something away from the speaker.

usage.desc: Movement TOWARD the speaker (come + bring).
Movement AWAY from the speaker (go + take).

examples: ✓ Bring the book here. (toward me)
✓ Take this to school. (away from me)
✗ Take your umbrella when you come here.

title: It's vs. Its
explain: It's is a contraction of 'It is' or 'It has'. Its (no apostrophe) is the possessive form, showing that something belongs to 'it'.

usage.desc: Contraction = 'It is' or 'It has'.
Possessive — belonging to it (no apostrophe).

examples: ✓ It's raining outside. (It is raining)
✓ The cat licked its paw. (belonging to the cat)
✗ The dog wagged it's tail.

title: Affect vs. Effect
explain: Affect is usually a verb meaning 'to influence'. Effect is usually a noun meaning 'the result or outcome'.

usage.desc: Verb — to influence or have an impact on.
Noun — the result, outcome, or consequence.

examples: ✓ The news affected me deeply. (verb)
✓ It had a bad effect on my mood. (noun)
✗ The medicine had a good affect.

title: Than vs. Then
explain: Than is used for comparisons. Then refers to time — what happened next, or at a particular time.

usage.desc: Comparison — used with comparatives.
Time — 'next', 'after that', 'at that time'.

examples: ✓ She is taller than me.
✓ Finish this, then go.
✗ He is smarter then his brother.

title: Either vs. Neither
explain: Both refer to two things or people. Either means one or the other (positive choice). Neither means not one and not the other (negative).

usage.desc: One of two — any one (positive option).
None of two — not one, not the other (negative).

examples: ✓ Either option works for me.
✓ Neither boy came to the party.
✗ Neither of the options are correct. → is correct

title: May vs. Might
explain: Both express possibility, but they differ in the degree of likelihood. May shows higher probability; Might shows lower probability or more uncertainty.

usage.desc: Higher possibility — about 70% likely.
Lower possibility — about 30% likely.

examples: ✓ It may rain today. (quite likely)
✓ He might come. (less certain)
✓ She might have told the truth. (past possibility)

title: Lie vs. Lay
explain: Lie means to rest or recline (no object needed). Lay means to put something down (needs an object). These are frequently confused — especially in past tense.

usage.desc: To rest — no object. (lie, lay, lain)
To put something — needs an object. (lay, laid, laid)

examples: ✓ I lie on the bed to rest.
✓ I laid the book on the table yesterday.
✓ Let him lie down for a while.
✗ He lies the phone on the table.

title: Advice vs. Advise
explain: Advice is a noun — the recommendation itself. Advise is a verb — the act of giving advice. The pronunciation difference helps: advice (s-sound) vs. advise (z-sound).

usage.desc: Noun — a piece of advice, good advice.
Verb — to advise someone, I advise you.

examples: ✓ Give me some advice. (noun)
✓ I advise you to study hard. (verb)
✗ He gave me a great advise.

title: Their / There / They're
explain: Three homophones (same sound, different meaning). Context determines which one to use.

usage.desc: Possessive — belonging to them.
Place — at that location.
Contraction — 'They are'.

examples: ✓ Their house is very big.
✓ Go there and wait.
✓ They're planning their vacation over there.
✗ There coming tomorrow.

title: Too vs. Very
explain: Too implies excess — something is beyond an acceptable limit, often with a negative consequence. Very is simply an intensifier with no negative connotation.

usage.desc: Excess — beyond the acceptable limit (negative consequence).
High degree — just intensifies the adjective (neutral/positive).

examples: ✓ The tea is too hot to drink. (can't drink it)
✓ The movie was very interesting!
✗ The tea is very hot to drink.

title: Beside vs. Besides
explain: Beside means physically next to something. Besides means in addition to something. One letter makes a huge difference in meaning.

usage.desc: Next to — physical position.
In addition to — extra information.

examples: ✓ Sit beside me. (next to me)
✓ Besides math, I also love science. (in addition)
✗ He sat besides me for dinner.
trick: Beside = Next to (think: side by side) | Besides = Plus / Also

title: Farther vs. Further
explain: Farther refers to physical, measurable distance. Further refers to figurative extension — more of something abstract like discussion, education, or explanation.

usage.desc: Physical, literal distance you can measure.
Figurative — more, additional, deeper.

examples: ✓ We walked farther than usual today.
✓ No further discussion is needed.
✓ We need further clarification.
✗ He threw the ball further than me.

title: Despite vs. In Spite Of
explain: Both mean the same thing ('even though') and are followed by a noun or gerund (-ing word). The key difference is structural: Despite has no 'of'; In Spite Of requires 'of'.

usage.desc: No 'of' → Despite + noun/gerund.
Requires 'of' → In spite of + noun/gerund.

examples: ✓ Despite the rain, we played.
✓ In spite of being tired, he worked.
✗ Despite of the cold, I wore shorts.
trick: No 'of' after Despite | 'of' is required in In spite of

title: Although / Though / Even Though
explain: All three are conjunctions showing contrast ('but / however'). They vary in strength. Each must be followed by a full clause (subject + verb). Don't add 'but' or 'yet' after them.

usage.desc: Standard contrast — followed by full clause.
Informal version of although; can end a sentence.
Strongest contrast — used for surprising facts.

examples: ✓ Although it was raining, we went out.
✓ Even though he is rich, he is humble.
✗ Although he is old, but he runs fast.
trick: Even though > Although > Though (in strength of contrast)

title: While vs. When
explain: While is used for actions that span a duration of time (ongoing). When is used for a specific moment or point in time.

usage.desc: Duration — two actions happening at the same time.
A specific moment — one action at a precise point.

examples: ✓ I was studying while it rained. (parallel ongoing)
✓ Call me when you reach. (specific moment)
✓ I met her when she was shopping.

title: Unless vs. If Not
explain: Unless already means 'if not', so never use 'not' with unless — it creates a double negative. Always use the positive form of the verb after unless.

usage.desc: = 'If not' — negative condition without 'not'.
= Can be used separately but never combine with 'unless'.

examples: ✓ Unless you study, you will fail.
✓ You can't enter unless you show ID.
✗ Unless you don't study, you will fail. (double negative)
trick: Unless is already negative — never add 'not' after it!

title: Because / Since / As
explain: All three show cause or reason, but differ in strength and usage. Because gives the strongest, most direct reason. Since and As suggest the reason is already known.

usage.desc: Strong, direct reason — often the main focus.
Reason is known/secondary — also has a time sense.
Soft reason — both things happening at the same time.

examples: ✓ He left because he was ill. (main reason)
✓ Since you're here, let's begin. (known reason)
✓ As it was late, we stayed.

title: Due To vs. Because Of
explain: Both show reason, but their grammatical positions differ. Due to follows a 'be' verb and modifies a noun. Because of introduces the reason before the main action.

usage.desc: After a 'be' verb (is, was, were) — modifies a noun.
Before an action verb — introduces the reason.

examples: ✓ His absence was due to illness. (after 'was')
✓ He missed class because of illness. (before action)
✗ He left due to he was sick.
trick: Due to = Comes after is/was | Because of = Before the action

title: Who vs. That (Relative Clauses)
explain: Who is exclusively for people. That works as a universal connector for people, animals, and things. Use 'who' when you want to specifically humanize.

usage.desc: Only for people — person-specific.
Universal — people, animals, things.

examples: ✓ The girl who sang won the prize.
✓ The singer that impressed us was her.
✓ The car that I drive is electric.

title: Each Other vs. One Another
explain: Each other is used when exactly two people or things are involved in a mutual action. One another is used when three or more are involved.

usage.desc: Exactly 2 people — mutual action between two.
3 or more people — mutual action in a group.

examples: ✓ Ram and Shyam respect each other.
✓ The team members helped one another.
✓ Friends must support one another.

title: Hard vs. Hardly
explain: Hard means with great effort or intensity (works as both adjective and adverb). Hardly is a negative adverb meaning 'barely' or 'almost not at all'.

usage.desc: Adverb — with effort, intensely, diligently.
Negative adverb — barely, almost not, scarcely.

examples: ✓ She works hard. (with effort)
✓ I hardly know him. (barely)
✗ He works hardly every day.
trick: Hard = A lot of effort | Hardly = Barely / almost not

title: Since vs. Because
explain: When used as conjunctions of reason, Since implies the reason is already known to both parties (less emphasis). Because gives new, direct, or emphatic reason.

usage.desc: Reason is known or background — casual.
Clear, strong, or new reason — direct.

examples: ✓ Since you're here, let's talk.
✓ He came because he was invited.
✓ I couldn't come because I was busy.
trick: Use Since when the cause is known or secondary

title: Not Only…But Also
explain: Not only…but also is a correlative conjunction pair. For correct grammar, ensure both parts have the same grammatical structure (parallel structure).

usage.desc: Both sides must match — noun:noun OR verb:verb OR adjective:adjective.

examples: ✓ She is not only smart but also hardworking. (adj:adj)
✓ He not only sings but also dances. (verb:verb)
✗ Not only he sings, but also dances.

title: So That vs. In Order That
explain: Both express purpose — why something is done. They are followed by a subject + modal verb (can, may, might, could, would).

usage.desc: Common — followed by subject + modal verb.
Formal — same meaning, more literary.

examples: ✓ He studies so that he can pass.
✓ She trained in order that she may win.
✓ I left early so that I could catch the bus.

title: Even If vs. Even Though
explain: Even if introduces a hypothetical or imaginary condition (might not happen). Even though introduces a real, factual condition (it actually happened or is happening).

usage.desc: Imaginary / conditional — may or may not happen.
Reality / factual — it actually is or was true.

examples: ✓ I'll come even if it rains. (condition — might rain)
✓ I came even though it was raining. (reality — it was raining)
✓ I'll go even if it rains.

title: Unless vs. Until
explain: Unless is about condition (if not this, then that). Until is about time (up to a certain point in time). These are completely different words often confused.

usage.desc: Condition — 'If not'. Subject: will/won't happen.
Time — 'up to the point when'. Ongoing till a moment.

examples: ✓ Unless you study, you'll fail. (condition)
✓ Wait here until I come. (time)
✗ Wait here unless I come.

title: Too…To vs. So…That
explain: Too…to expresses excess that prevents an action — negative outcome implied. So…that shows the degree of something and its actual result.

usage.desc: Too + adj + to + verb = Can't do it (negative).
So + adj + that + result = It happened (positive/neutral).

examples: ✓ He is too weak to walk. (can't walk)
✓ He was so weak that he fell. (did fall)
✓ She is too tired to continue.

title: As If vs. As Though
explain: Both As if and As though mean 'in a way that suggests' — they introduce unreal or imaginary situations. Use past tense after them even for present scenarios.

usage.desc: Both express unreal appearance or imagination. Use past tense after them.

examples: ✓ He behaves as if he were a king. (imaginary)
✓ She talks as though she knew everything.
✗ He acts as if he is the boss. (should be: were)
trick: Both express false/imaginary situations → Always use past tense after them

title: No Sooner…Than
explain: No sooner…than expresses that one action happened immediately after another. It requires subject-auxiliary inversion — the helping verb comes before the subject.

usage.desc: No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than + V2 (past)

examples: ✓ No sooner had he arrived than it started raining.
✓ No sooner had I called than she cried.
✗ No sooner I had called than she cried.
trick: No sooner needs inversion: had + subject + V3 + than

title: Scarcely / Hardly / Barely…When
explain: Like 'No sooner…than', these words also show two quick successive actions. They require subject-auxiliary inversion and are always paired with 'when' (not 'than').

usage.desc: Hardly/Scarcely/Barely + had + subject + V3 + when + V2

examples: ✓ Hardly had she left when he arrived.
✓ Scarcely had I reached when it started.
✗ Hardly he had entered when the lights went off.

title: So vs. Such
explain: So intensifies adjectives and adverbs directly. Such intensifies a noun phrase (adjective + noun) or a noun alone.

usage.desc: So + adjective/adverb.
Such + (a/an) + adjective + noun.

examples: ✓ She is so beautiful.
✓ It was such a beautiful day.
✓ He is so smart. / It was such a good movie.
✗ It was so a beautiful day.

title: As vs. Like
explain: As shows the actual role someone plays (used with subject + verb). Like shows similarity or comparison (used with nouns/pronouns, no verb).

usage.desc: Actual role — followed by subject + verb.
Similarity — followed by noun/pronoun only.

examples: ✓ He works as a teacher. (that IS his role)
✓ He sings like a professional. (comparison)
✗ Do as I say, not like I say.

title: All vs. Whole
explain: All is used with plural or uncountable nouns to mean 'every one of'. Whole is used with singular countable nouns to mean 'complete/entire'.

usage.desc: Plural / uncountable — all students, all water.
Singular countable — the whole class, the whole apple.

examples: ✓ All people were silent.
✓ The whole class was present.
✓ I ate all the apples. / I ate the whole apple.

title: One of the + Plural Noun + Singular Verb
explain: When the subject is 'One of the + plural noun', the verb must be singular because it agrees with 'one', not with the plural noun.

usage.desc: One of the [plural noun] + singular verb (has, is, was, does)

examples: ✓ One of the boys has won.
✓ One of the best books I've read.
✗ One of the boys have won.
trick: 'One of' = The subject is ONE → always use singular verb

title: The Number vs. A Number
explain: 'The number' acts as a singular subject. 'A number of' acts as a plural subject. One article makes all the difference!

usage.desc: Singular — use 'is, was, has'.
Plural — use 'are, were, have'.

examples: ✓ The number of students is high.
✓ A number of students are missing.
✗ A number of students is present.

title: Neither of / Either of → Singular
explain: Even though 'of' is followed by a plural noun, the verbs after neither of and either of must always be singular because neither/either is singular.

usage.desc: Neither of / Either of + plural noun → singular verb

examples: ✓ Neither of the boys is present.
✓ Either of the options is fine.
✗ Neither of the girls are dancing.

title: One / None — Singular or Plural?
explain: One is always singular. None is flexible — singular when referring to uncountable nouns, but can be plural when referring to countable/people.

usage.desc: Always singular.
Usually singular (uncountable); can be plural (countable/people).

examples: ✓ One of them is coming.
✓ None of the food is left. (uncountable)
✓ None of the students are present. (countable — acceptable)
trick: One = Always singular | None = Both accepted, context matters

title: Each of + Plural Noun = Singular Verb
explain: Even though the noun after 'each of' is plural, the verb must be singular. 'Each' focuses on individuals — one at a time.

usage.desc: Each of + plural noun → singular verb (is, has, was)

examples: ✓ Each of the girls is dancing.
✓ Each of the boys has done well.
✗ Each of the players are excited.
trick: Each of = Think about one at a time → singular verb

title: Relative Pronoun Agreement
explain: When a relative pronoun (who, which, that) is used, its verb must agree with the noun it refers to (the antecedent) — not with the pronoun itself.

usage.desc: Check what the relative pronoun refers to → match verb to that noun.

examples: ✓ She is one of the girls who dance well. (girls → plural → dance)
✓ It is I who am responsible. (I → am)
✗ She is one of the girls who dances well.
trick: Check what 'who/which/that' refers to → match verb with that noun

title: Not Only…But Also — Parallel Structure
explain: The correlative conjunction Not only…but also requires the same grammatical structure on both sides — this is called parallel structure.

usage.desc: Match grammar on both sides: verb:verb, noun:noun, adj:adj.

examples: ✓ Not only is she smart, but she is also kind. (adj:adj)
✓ He not only sings but also dances. (verb:verb)
✗ Not only he sings, but also dances.

title: As Well As — Verb Agreement
explain: As well as does not create a compound subject. The verb agrees ONLY with the first (main) subject, ignoring the phrase introduced by 'as well as'.

usage.desc: Verb agrees with first subject only. The 'as well as' phrase is parenthetical.

examples: ✓ Ram, as well as his friends, is coming. (Ram = singular)
✓ She as well as her sisters is beautiful.
✗ Ram as well as his friends are coming.
trick: Ignore 'as well as ...' → Verb agrees with the first subject only

title: Rather Than — Parallel Structure
explain: Rather than requires the same form (verb form, tense) on both sides of the comparison. Keep both sides parallel for correct grammar.

usage.desc: Same tense/form on both sides of 'rather than'.

examples: ✓ I prefer tea rather than coffee. (noun:noun)
✓ He works rather than plays. (verb:verb)
✗ I would rather sleeping home than going out.
trick: Use same tense/form on both sides of 'rather than'

title: No Sooner…Than — Inversion
explain: When the sentence begins with 'No sooner', subject-auxiliary inversion is required. The helping verb 'had' comes before the subject.

usage.desc: No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than + past verb

examples: ✓ No sooner had I reached than the train left.
✓ No sooner had he come than it rained.
✗ No sooner I reached than the train left.

title: One of the Most + Superlative + Plural Noun
explain: After 'One of the most/best/worst', always use a plural noun — even though 'one' is singular. The plural noun is the group, and 'one' is chosen from it.

usage.desc: One of the + superlative + plural noun

examples: ✓ One of the most intelligent students in the class.
✓ One of the best books I've ever read.
✗ One of the best book I've read.

title: So That — Purpose Clause
explain: So that introduces a purpose clause. After 'so that', use a subject plus a modal verb (can, may, might, could, would) — never use an infinitive directly.

usage.desc: So that + subject + can/may/might/could + base verb

examples: ✓ He studies hard so that he can succeed.
✓ She left early so that she could catch the bus.
✗ He studies so that succeed.

title: Because Of vs. Due To (Detailed)
explain: Both show reason, but they attach differently in a sentence. Due to modifies a noun (often after 'be' verbs). Because of shows the cause of an action.

usage.desc: Comes after a 'be' verb — His failure was due to laziness.
Comes before an action — He failed because of laziness.

examples: ✓ He failed because of laziness.
✓ His failure was due to laziness.
✗ He left due to he was sick.
trick: Due to = Noun cause | Because of = Verb cause

title: Each Other vs. One Another (Review)
explain: A review: Each other for exactly two people involved in a mutual action. One another for groups of three or more.

usage.desc: 2 people — mutual action between two.
3+ people — mutual action in a group.

examples: ✓ Ram and Shyam help each other.
✓ We must support one another.
✓ The three boys fought one another.

title: Too…To — Inability
explain: Too…to structure expresses that something is in excess and therefore prevents an action. The result is always negative (inability).

usage.desc: Too + adjective + to + base verb = cannot do it

examples: ✓ He is too weak to walk.
✓ It's too cold to go outside.
✓ She's too tired to continue.
✗ He is too much weak to run.
trick: Too + adj + to + verb = Impossible / can't do it

title: So…That — Result
explain: So…that structure shows intensity leading to a specific result. Unlike 'too...to', the result actually happens.

usage.desc: So + adjective + that + subject + verb (result)

examples: ✓ He was so tired that he slept instantly.
✓ The movie was so boring that I left.
✓ It was so hot that I fainted.
✗ He was so tired that sleep instantly.
trick: So + adj + that = the result actually happened

title: Hardly/Scarcely…When — Inversion
explain: When 'Hardly' or 'Scarcely' begins a sentence, inversion is required: 'had' comes before the subject. Always paired with 'when', not 'than'.

usage.desc: Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + V3 + when + V2

examples: ✓ Hardly had he arrived when it started raining.
✓ Scarcely had I slept when the phone rang.
✗ Hardly he had entered when the lights went off.

title: Too Much vs. Much Too
explain: Though they look similar, their positions differ. Too much comes before nouns. Much too comes before adjectives or adverbs.

usage.desc: Before nouns — too much noise, too much food.
Before adjectives/adverbs — much too difficult, much too late.

examples: ✓ There is too much noise here.
✓ This is much too difficult for me.
✗ He is too much tired.

title: Lest — Negative Purpose
explain: Lest means 'for fear that' or 'in case … not'. It expresses a negative purpose — you do something to prevent something bad. Always use 'should' after lest.

usage.desc: Lest + subject + should + base verb

examples: ✓ Walk carefully lest you should fall.
✓ Study now lest you should fail.
✓ Lest she should fall, I held her hand.
✗ Work hard lest you may fail.
trick: Lest = To prevent → always use should + base verb

title: Whether vs. If
explain: Whether is used when there are two alternatives or options. If is used for conditions — when something depends on something else happening.

usage.desc: Two alternatives — whether…or not.
Condition — if this happens, then that.

examples: ✓ I don't know whether he'll come or not.
✓ If it rains, we'll cancel the trip.
✓ We'll go whether it rains or not.
✗ I don't know either he'll attend or not.

title: Unless vs. Until (Review)
explain: A review of two commonly confused words: Unless introduces a condition (if not). Until introduces a point in time (up to when).

usage.desc: Condition — if not this, then that.
Time — continuing up to a certain moment.

examples: ✓ You won't pass unless you study.
✓ Wait until I return.
✗ Wait here unless I come back.
trick: Unless = If not (condition) | Until = Up to that time

title: As If / As Though — Past Tense
explain: When as if or as though introduces an unreal/imaginary situation, always use past tense — even when referring to the present.

usage.desc: As if / As though + past tense (even for present unreal situations)

examples: ✓ He behaves as if he were a king. (imaginary, so 'were')
✓ She talks as though she knew everything.
✗ He acts as if he is the boss. → should be 'were'
trick: As if / As though + imaginary = always use past tense (were)

title: Would Rather / Had Better
explain: Would rather expresses preference between two options. Had better gives strong advice — often implying a warning or consequence if not followed.

usage.desc: Preference — I would rather stay than go.
Strong advice/warning — you had better leave now.

examples: ✓ I would rather rest than work.
✓ You had better study now.
✓ I'd rather die than beg.
✗ He had better don't go now.

title: Hard vs. Hardly (Review)
explain: Review: Hard as an adverb means with great effort. Hardly is a negative adverb meaning barely or almost not at all. They are completely opposite in meaning.

usage.desc: With effort, diligently, intensely.
Barely, almost not, scarcely.

examples: ✓ He works hard every day.
✓ He hardly studies at all.
✓ I hardly know her.
trick: Hard = পরিশ্রম থেকে | Hardly = কঠিন থেকে / না এর সমান

title: Since vs. From
explain: Since refers to a definite point in the past and is used with perfect tenses. From indicates a starting point — for past or future — and is used with 'to/till/until'.

usage.desc: Point in past, with have/has/had — since Monday, since 2010.
Starting point with end time — from 9 AM to 5 PM.

examples: ✓ I've been here since Monday.
✓ The shop is open from 10 AM to 9 PM.
✗ I've been here from Monday.

title: Each / Every / All — Three-Way
explain: A three-way distinction: Each for individual focus (2 or more), Every for collective group (3 or more), All for the entire total group.

usage.desc: Individual — 2 or more, one at a time.
Group — 3 or more, all together.
Total — the entire group as a whole.

examples: ✓ Each player got a medal.
✓ Every student passed the exam.
✓ All players were excited.

title: As…As vs. So…As
explain: In comparisons of equality: as…as is used for positive sentences. In negative comparisons (with 'not'), traditionally not so…as is preferred (though 'not as…as' is also widely accepted).

usage.desc: Positive comparison — He is as tall as his brother.
Negative comparison — She is not so smart as you.

examples: ✓ He is as tall as his brother.
✓ She is not so smart as you.
✓ She is not as smart as you. (also correct)

title: Each of / Every One of → Singular
explain: Both 'Each of' and 'Every one of' must be followed by singular verbs, even though a plural noun follows 'of'.

usage.desc: Each of / Every one of + plural noun → singular verb

examples: ✓ Each of the boys has done well.
✓ Every one of them is ready.
✗ Each of the girls are dancing.
trick: 'Each of / Every one of' = Always singular verb

title: One vs. Ones
explain: One is used as a substitute for a singular countable noun. Ones substitutes for a plural countable noun. They avoid repetition of the noun.

usage.desc: Singular noun substitute.
Plural noun substitute.

examples: ✓ I want the red one. (one shirt)
✓ These are old pens. Take new ones. (plural)
✓ I like this shirt, but I prefer that one.

title: The Number vs. A Number (Review)
explain: Quick review: The number takes a singular verb. A number of takes a plural verb. The article determines everything.

usage.desc: Singular — The number of students is rising.
Plural — A number of people are missing.

examples: ✓ The number of students is rising.
✓ A number of students are missing.
✓ A number of people are present.

title: Both / Either / Neither — Three-Way
explain: A three-way distinction for pairs: Both = together (positive), Either = one of two (positive choice), Neither = none of two (negative).

usage.desc: Two together — positive. Both are here.
Any one of two — positive choice. Either seat is fine.
None of the two — negative. Neither answer is right.

examples: ✓ Both brothers are honest.
✓ You can take either seat.
✓ Neither answer is correct.

title: Gerunds — Verb as Noun
explain: Gerunds are formed by adding -ing to a verb. They function as nouns in a sentence — as subjects, objects, or after prepositions.

usage.desc: Verb + ing acting as a noun — swimming, reading, cooking.

examples: ✓ Swimming is good for health. (subject)
✓ I enjoy reading. (object)
✓ She is fond of singing. (after preposition)
trick: Gerund = Verb + ing → does the job of a NOUN

title: Infinitives — To + Verb
explain: Infinitives (to + base verb) express purpose, intention, or preference. They often come after verbs like want, refuse, agree, plan, hope, decide.

usage.desc: To + base verb — to learn, to come, to study.

examples: ✓ I want to learn English.
✓ He refused to come.
✓ I agreed to do the work.
trick: Infinitive = to + base verb → expresses purpose or intention

title: Double Negatives — Avoid!
explain: Using two negatives in one clause creates a double negative, which is grammatically incorrect in standard English. One negative is enough.

usage.desc: Don't use: not + nothing, not + nobody, don't + never.
Use: not + anything, not + anybody, don't + ever.

examples: ✓ I don't want anything.
✓ She didn't see anybody in the room.
✗ I don't want nothing. (double negative)
trick: Negative × Negative = Wrong! One negative is always enough.

title: Very / Much / Too — Intensifiers
explain: Each intensifier has a specific use: Very + adjective (neutral intensity), Much + past participle or comparative, Too = excessive (negative consequence).

usage.desc: Very + adjective/adverb — very good, very fast.
Much + past participle or comparative — much improved, much better.
Too + adjective — excess with negative result.

examples: ✓ Very good work!
✓ He is much improved since last month.
✓ Too expensive to buy.

title: Past Perfect — Two Past Actions
explain: The past perfect (had + V3) is used for an action that was completed BEFORE another action in the past. The earlier action uses past perfect; the later uses simple past.

usage.desc: Earlier action: had + V3 | Later action: simple past (V2)

examples: ✓ He had left before I arrived. (left = earlier)
✓ They had finished the game when it rained.
✓ When I reached, he had been waiting for an hour.
trick: Past perfect = 'had + V3' → action that happened first in the past

title: So That / In Order That — Purpose
explain: Both introduce purpose clauses. They explain WHY something is done. Follow them with a subject and modal verb for correct structure.

usage.desc: So that/In order that + subject + can/may/might/could + verb

examples: ✓ He studies hard so that he can succeed.
✓ She left early in order that she might catch the train.
✓ I work hard so that I could save money.
trick: Both = Purpose → always follow with modal verb (can/may/might)

title: Despite / Although / However
explain: Three different words all showing contrast, but used very differently. Despite = preposition, Although = conjunction (same sentence), However = adverb (separate sentence).

usage.desc: Preposition + noun/gerund — Despite being tired…
Conjunction + full clause — Although he was tired…
Adverb connecting two sentences — He was tired. However, he worked.

examples: ✓ Despite being tired, he worked.
✓ Although he was tired, he worked.
✓ He was tired. However, he worked.

title: Emphatic 'Do/Does/Did'
explain: Adding do/does/did to a positive sentence gives emphasis — it stresses that the action truly happened or is true. This is the emphatic use of auxiliaries.

usage.desc: I DO like chocolates. / He DID try his best.

examples: ✓ I do like chocolates! (emphasis)
✓ He did try his best. (past emphasis)
✓ She does study hard. (present emphasis)
trick: Add do/does/did to positive sentences for strong emphasis

title: Used To vs. Be Used To
explain: Used to describes a past habit that no longer continues. Be used to means to be accustomed to something (comfortable with it now, in the present).

usage.desc: Past habit no longer true — Used to + base verb.
Accustomed to now — be + used to + verb-ing/noun.

examples: ✓ I used to play cricket. (past habit, now stopped)
✓ I am used to getting up early. (accustomed now)
✓ I'm used to waking early.
trick: Used to = Past habit | Be used to = Comfortable now

title: Neither of / Either of / Both of
explain: Verb rules for these three: 'Neither of' and 'Either of' take singular verbs. 'Both of' takes a plural verb.

usage.desc: Singular verb — Neither of the boys has come.
Singular verb — Either of the answers is correct.
Plural verb — Both of them are ready.

examples: ✓ Neither of the boys has come.
✓ Either of the answers is correct.
✓ Both of them are ready.

title: If I Were / If He Were — Hypothetical
explain: In hypothetical or imaginary conditionals (Type 2), use were for ALL subjects — not 'was', even for singular subjects like I, he, she.

usage.desc: If + subject + were (for all persons — imaginary/unreal)

examples: ✓ If I were you, I'd study more.
✓ If he were rich, he'd travel.
✓ He behaves as if he were a king.
✗ If I was you, I'd study more.

title: By / Until / Till — Time Prepositions
explain: By means before or at a deadline. Until/Till means continuing up to a point in time. 'Until' and 'Till' mean the same thing.

usage.desc: Deadline — before or at that time.
Ongoing — up to that moment.

examples: ✓ Finish it by Monday. (deadline)
✓ Wait until I come. (ongoing till that moment)
✗ I will wait by you come back.

title: Would Have + V3 — Unreal Past
explain: Would have + V3 is used in Type 3 conditionals (third conditional) to talk about unreal past situations — things that didn't happen but could have.

usage.desc: If had + V3 → would have + V3

examples: ✓ I would have helped you, but I was busy.
✓ She would have come if she had known.
✓ If I had worked hard, I would have passed.
trick: Would have + V3 = Imagined past / things that didn't happen

title: Not Only…But Also — Parallel (Review)
explain: Review: 'Not only…but also' is a correlative pair requiring parallel structure. The grammatical form on both sides must match.

usage.desc: Match grammar → verb:verb, noun:noun, adj:adj

examples: ✓ Not only intelligent but also hardworking. (adj:adj)
✓ Not only does he dance, but he also sings.
✗ Not only he sings, but also dances.

title: Much / Very Much / Too Much
explain: Three related but distinct intensifiers: Much = quantity. Very much = strong emphasis (degree). Too much = excessive (a problem).

usage.desc: Quantity — There isn't much time.
Intensity — I like it very much.
Excessive (negative) — He ate too much food.

examples: ✓ He ate too much food.
✓ I like it very much.
✓ There isn't much time.

title: Hard vs. Hardly (Hindi Trick)
explain: Final review with Hindi keywords: Hard = পরিশ্রম থেকে (with effort). Hardly = কঠিন থেকে / না এর সমান (barely/scarcely).

usage.desc: With great effort — works hard, tries hard.
Barely, almost not — hardly knows, hardly works.

examples: ✓ He works hard.
✓ I hardly know her.
✓ He hardly studies. (barely studies)

title: So vs. Such (Review)
explain: Review: So comes before adjectives/adverbs alone. Such comes before noun phrases (adjective + noun).

usage.desc: So + adj/adverb — He is so smart.
Such + (a/an) + adj + noun — It was such a good movie.

examples: ✓ He is so smart.
✓ It was such a good movie.
✓ She such a beautiful singer that she won.
✗ It was so a beautiful day.

title: Much / Many / A Lot Of
explain: Much = uncountable. Many = countable. A lot of = works with BOTH countable and uncountable nouns. When unsure, use 'a lot of'.

usage.desc: Uncountable — much sugar, much water, much time.
Countable — many students, many books, many cars.
Both — a lot of money, a lot of students.

examples: ✓ Much sugar. ✓ Many students. ✓ A lot of money.
✓ There are a lot of people outside.
✗ How many sugar do you need?
trick: Not sure? Use A lot of — it works everywhere!

title: Even / Even Though / Even If
explain: Three related phrases: Even = emphasis. Even though = surprising real fact. Even if = imaginary condition.

usage.desc: Emphasis — Even a child knows this.
Surprising reality — I came even though I was sick.
Imaginary condition — I'll go even if it rains.

examples: ✓ Even a child knows this.
✓ I came even though I was sick.
✓ I'll go even if it rains.

title: Else / Other / Another
explain: Three words that indicate 'something different': Else = different person/thing. Other = the remaining one(s). Another = one more of the same.

usage.desc: Different person/thing — someone else, somewhere else.
The remaining — the other option, other students.
One more — another pen, another day.

examples: ✓ Someone else called.
✓ The other option is better.
✓ Give me another pen.
trick: Another = Extra one | Other = Different remaining | Else = Different person/thing

title: Hope vs. Wish
explain: Hope is used for real, possible situations in the future. Wish is used for unreal, impossible, or regretful situations (contrary to fact).

usage.desc: Real possibility — I hope you pass.
Unreal / impossible — I wish I were taller.

examples: ✓ I hope you pass. (it's possible)
✓ I wish I were taller. (I'm not, unreal)
✓ I wish I had studied harder. (regret about past)

title: Too vs. Enough
explain: Too means more than required — excess, negative outcome. Enough means sufficient — just the right amount, positive outcome.

usage.desc: Excess — too + adjective + to + verb (can't do it).
Sufficient — adjective + enough + to + verb (can do it).

examples: ✓ He is too tired to work. (can't work)
✓ She is smart enough to win. (can win)
✓ He is strong enough to lift it.

title: Gerunds vs. Infinitives — Verb Choice
explain: Some verbs are always followed by gerunds, some by infinitives. Knowing which verb takes which form prevents common errors.

usage.desc: enjoy, avoid, mind, suggest, finish, deny, consider.
want, plan, hope, agree, refuse, decide, manage.

examples: ✓ I enjoy swimming. (enjoy + gerund)
✓ I want to swim. (want + infinitive)
✓ She suggested leaving early.

title: Due To vs. Because Of (Review)
explain: Final review: Both show reason, but 'Due to' is more formal and follows 'be' verbs. 'Because of' is used before the action in casual or direct causation.

usage.desc: Formal — caused by (after is/was).
Casual — reason (before action verb).

examples: ✓ The flight was delayed due to rain.
✓ He failed because of laziness.
✗ He left due to he was sick.
trick: 'Due to' = Formal (after be verb) | 'Because of' = Casual (reason)

title: Each Other vs. One Another (Final)
explain: Final review: The rule is clear and consistent. Always use 'each other' for two, 'one another' for three or more.

usage.desc: 2 people — mutual between two.
3+ people — mutual in a group.

examples: ✓ Ram and Shyam help each other.
✓ Friends must support one another.
✗ The three boys fought each other.

title: Sometime / Sometimes / Some Time
explain: Three different words, all pronounced similarly. Each has a distinct meaning: unspecified time, occasionally, or a period of time.

usage.desc: Unspecified/vague time — Let's meet sometime.
Occasionally — I sometimes eat out.
A period/duration — I need some time to think.

examples: ✓ Let's meet sometime next week.
✓ I sometimes eat out.
✓ I need some time to think.
trick: Sometime = কখন? | Sometimes = মাঝে মাঝে | Some time = সামান্য সময়

title: Since vs. From (Review)
explain: Review: Since marks a point in the past and is used with perfect tenses. From marks a starting point and needs a paired 'to/till/until'.

usage.desc: Past point → to now — with have/has/had.
Start point + end — from 9 to 5, from Monday to Friday.

examples: ✓ I have lived here since 2010.
✓ I worked from 9 AM to 5 PM.
✗ I've been here from Monday.
trick: Since = Past → Now (with perfect tense) | From = Start + end time

title: All vs. Whole (Review)
explain: Review: All is used with plural or uncountable nouns. Whole is used with a singular countable noun to mean 'entire/complete'.

usage.desc: Plural or total — all the apples, all the people.
One complete unit — the whole apple, the whole day.

examples: ✓ I ate all the apples.
✓ I ate the whole apple.
✓ All the students passed.
trick: Whole = One complete item | All = Many or the total

title: Hardly / Barely / Scarcely — Negative Adverbs
explain: All three mean 'almost not' and carry negative meaning. Never combine them with other negatives (not, no, never) — it creates double negatives.

usage.desc: Almost not — I could hardly walk.
Almost not — He barely passed.
Almost not — We scarcely met.

examples: ✓ I could hardly walk.
✓ He barely passed the exam.
✓ We scarcely met.
✗ I couldn't hardly walk. (double negative)
trick: All three = Negative → avoid double negatives with them

title: That vs. Which — Essential vs. Extra Info
explain: That introduces essential (defining) information — removing it changes the meaning. Which introduces extra (non-defining) information — set off by commas.

usage.desc: Essential info — no commas. The car that I bought is red.
Extra info — with commas. The car, which I bought last year, is red.

examples: ✓ The car that I bought is red. (essential — which car)
✓ The car, which I bought last year, is red. (extra info)
✗ The car which I bought is red. (no comma — should be 'that')

title: Yet / Still / Already
explain: Three time adverbs often confused: Still = something continuing. Yet = something not happened (in questions/negatives). Already = something happened before expected.

usage.desc: Continuing — She is still sleeping.
Not happened (questions/negatives) — Have you eaten yet?
Happened before expected — I've already done it.

examples: ✓ She is still sleeping.
✓ Have you eaten yet?
✓ I've already done it.
✓ He hasn't arrived yet.
trick: Still = এখনো ও | Yet = এখন পর্যন্ত না | Already = আগে থেকে হয় গেছে

title: Few / Less / Several
explain: Three quantity words: Few = countable (negative tone). Several = countable (more than a few, neutral/positive). Less = uncountable.

usage.desc: Countable, negative — Few people came.
Countable, more than few — Several students passed.
Uncountable — Less water is left.

examples: ✓ Few people came. (almost none)
✓ Several students passed. (more than a few)
✓ Less water is left.

title: Whoever vs. Whomever
explain: Whoever is the subject form. Whomever is the object form. Apply the He/Him test: if 'He' fits, use Whoever; if 'Him' fits, use Whomever.

usage.desc: Subject (He) — Whoever comes is welcome.
Object (Him) — Invite whomever you want.

examples: ✓ Whoever comes is welcome. (He comes = Whoever)
✓ Invite whomever you want. (You want him = Whomever)

title: When / While / As — Time Conjunctions
explain: Three time conjunctions: When = single/specific action, While = two ongoing parallel actions, As = simultaneous actions (often cause-and-effect).

usage.desc: Specific moment — I was sleeping when he called.
Parallel ongoing — I was cooking while she was studying.
Simultaneous — As I walked in, she left.

examples: ✓ I was sleeping when he called.
✓ I was cooking while she was studying.
✓ As I walked in, she left.

title: At / In / On — Time Prepositions
explain: The three main time prepositions: At for exact times, On for days and dates, In for months, years, seasons, and longer periods.

usage.desc: Exact time — at 5 PM, at noon, at midnight.
Days and dates — on Monday, on 15th August.
Months, years, seasons — in March, in 2024, in winter.

examples: ✓ At 5 PM. ✓ On Monday. ✓ In March.
✓ I was born in 1999.
✓ The train arrives at 8 AM on Friday.

title: Suppose / Provided / Unless — Conditionals
explain: These words all introduce conditions: Suppose/Supposing = imagine this, Provided/Providing = only if, Unless = if not.

usage.desc: Imagine a condition — Suppose he comes late, what will you do?
Only if — Provided you work hard, you'll pass.
If not — You won't pass unless you study.

examples: ✓ Suppose he comes late, what will you do?
✓ Provided you work hard, you'll pass.
✓ You won't pass unless you study.

title: Much Too vs. Too Much (Review)
explain: Review: Much too comes before adjectives/adverbs. Too much comes before nouns. Position determines which to use.

usage.desc: Before adjective/adverb — He is much too lazy.
Before noun — I ate too much food.

examples: ✓ He is much too lazy.
✓ I ate too much food.
✗ He is too much lazy.

title: So That / In Order That (Review)
explain: Review: Both mean 'for the purpose of'. Always follow with a modal verb (can, could, may, might) and then the base verb.

usage.desc: So that / In order that + subject + modal (can/may/could/might) + verb

examples: ✓ I studied so that I could pass.
✓ She left early in order that she might catch the train.
✓ He works hard so that he can succeed.
trick: Use modal can/could/may/might after 'so that/in order that'

title: In Case vs. If
explain: In case = taking precaution against something that might happen. If = a condition — something happens BECAUSE of something else.

usage.desc: Precaution — take umbrella in case it rains (it might).
Condition — I'll go if he comes (only then).

examples: ✓ Take an umbrella in case it rains. (precaution)
✓ I'll go if he comes. (condition)
✗ I'll take an umbrella if it may rain.

title: As If / As Though (Review)
explain: Review: Both 'as if' and 'as though' are used for unreal/imaginative situations. They are interchangeable and always followed by past tense.

usage.desc: Unreal/imaginative + past tense

examples: ✓ He talks as if he were a king.
✓ She smiled as though nothing had happened.
✗ He acts as if he is the boss.
trick: Use past tense after 'as if / as though' for unreal things

title: Had Better / Would Rather (Review)
explain: Review: Had better gives strong advice or warning (there will be a consequence). Would rather expresses preference between two choices.

usage.desc: Strong warning/advice — You had better study now.
Preference — I would rather sleep than work.

examples: ✓ You had better study now. (warning)
✓ I would rather stay home than go out. (preference)
✗ He had better don't go now.

title: Because vs. So — Not Together!
explain: Never use 'because' and 'so' in the same sentence — they both show cause and result. Use one or the other, not both, as it creates a redundant double connector.

usage.desc: He was tired because he was ill, so he slept.
He was tired because he was ill. OR: He was ill, so he slept.

examples: ✓ He was tired because he was ill.
✓ He was ill, so he slept.
✗ He was tired because he was ill, so he slept.
trick: Use either Because OR So — NEVER both in one sentence!

title: No Sooner…Than / Hardly…When (Review)
explain: Review: Two quick actions in rapid succession. 'No sooner' pairs with 'than'; 'Hardly/Scarcely' pairs with 'when'. Both require subject-auxiliary inversion with 'had'.

usage.desc: No sooner had + subject + V3 + than + V2
Hardly had + subject + V3 + when + V2

examples: ✓ No sooner had he come than it rained.
✓ Hardly had I slept when the phone rang.
✗ Hardly had he arrived than it started.

title: Each Other vs. One Another (Three-Peat)
explain: One more review to cement the rule: 'Each other' is strictly for two. 'One another' is for three or more. This is a common exam question.

usage.desc: 2 people — Ram and Shyam respect each other.
3+ people — We should all help one another.

examples: ✓ Ram and Shyam respect each other.
✓ We should all help one another.
✗ The three friends fought each other.

title: Emphatic Pronouns
explain: Emphatic pronouns (myself, yourself, himself, herself, ourselves, themselves) are used after the subject to add emphasis and stress. They are NOT reflexive here — they emphasize, not reflect the action.

usage.desc: I myself, she herself, he himself — used after subject for stress.
She hurt herself — the subject receives the action.

examples: ✓ I myself completed the work. (emphasis)
✓ She herself cooked the food.
✓ The principal himself took the class.
✗ I myself was hurt. (reflexive, not emphatic)
trick: Emphatic pronouns come after the subject to add stress — not as an object
